To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
1) CDKN2A variants may predispose to melanoma, breast cancer and lung cancers.

the CDKN2a, XPD and the MC1R genes do not contribute significantly in the context of familial melanoma or familial breast cancer but they may predispose to sporadic melanoma, early onset breast cancer and/or lung cancer.
common variants of genes predisposing to malignant melanoma (CDKN2A, ARF, XPD, MC1R) do not contribute significantly, if at all, to familial melanoma, but may predispose to other cancers.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the molecular basis of cancer susceptibility and the development of molecular tests for the identification of cancer predisposing genes and the assessment of the clinical value of such tests.

the identification of genetic variants that contribute to the risk of malignant melanoma and breast and colorectal cancer in the Polish population, and the evaluation of their potential clinical utility.
the identification of genetic factors that may predispose to breast and malignant melanoma.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the contribution of the CDKN, XPD and MCR genes to the development of malignant melanoma and breast cancers is not significant, but that common variants of these genes are associated with increased cancer risk in a small proportion of patients.
the common variants of CDKN2A (A148T), XPD (R478W, R561H and D751Y) and MC1R (V60L,R151C,R163Q and R161W) may be associated with increased risk of malignant melanoma and early onset breast cancer.
the common CDKN2A A148T variant may predispose to melanoma, breast and lung cancer, and the XPD variants and the common MC1R variants may predispose to breast cancer and melanoma.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the genetic factors for malignant melanoma and breast cancers are not identical, and the common genetic variants that we have found to be associated with these cancers are likely to be involved in a complex network of genetic and environmental factors.

genetic testing for CDKN2A variants is not recommended for patients with familial malignant melanoma and breast carcinoma, while XPD and MCIR variants may be of some importance for breast cancer risk and malignant melanoma.
the common genetic variants studied in the present thesis are associated with increased risk of malignant melanoma, but their contribution to familial breast cancer risk seems to be small.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the study of the genetic basis of cancer predisposition is a complex task, and it is not always easy to separate the wheat from the chaff.
the genetic factors predisposing to melanoma and breast cancers may overlap and that the genetic basis of cancer predisposition is complex.
the common variants in the CDKN2, XPD and the MC1R genes may predispose to breast cancer, malignant melanoma and lung cancer.
